questions.prompt: The sliding-window technique reduces which kind of brute-force solution to linear time?

options.text: Recomputing an aggregate over every contiguous subarray from scratch

questions.explanation: Instead of an O(n^2) or worse pass over all subarrays, the window updates its aggregate incrementally as it slides, adding the entering element and removing the leaving one in O(1).

questions.prompt: For the longest substring without repeating characters, a variable-size sliding window uses which auxiliary structure?

options.text: A hash set or last-seen index map for characters in the window

questions.explanation: Tracking which characters are currently in the window lets the left edge jump past a repeat in O(1). Each character enters and leaves the window at most once, so the scan is O(n).

questions.prompt: A prefix-sum array lets you answer the sum of any subarray A[l..r] in:
questions.explanation: With prefix sums P, the range sum is P[r+1] - P[l], a constant-time subtraction after building P in linear time. This trades a one-time O(n) cost for O(1) queries.

questions.prompt: To count subarrays whose sum equals a target k, the efficient approach combines prefix sums with:

options.text: A hash map of prefix-sum frequencies seen so far
A binary search tree of the elements

questions.explanation: At each index the number of earlier prefix sums equal to current - k gives the subarrays ending here. A hash map of prefix-sum counts makes the whole scan O(n).

questions.prompt: The sliding-window-maximum problem (maximum of every window of size k) is solved in O(n) using:

options.text: A monotonic deque holding candidate indices in decreasing value order

questions.explanation: The deque keeps indices whose values are useful future maxima, discarding smaller trailing ones. Its front is always the current window's maximum, and each index is pushed and popped once.

questions.prompt: Why does the classic sliding-window minimum-length-subarray technique require the values to be non-negative?

options.text: Prefix sums do not exist for negatives
The window size must be even
Shrinking the window must monotonically decrease the sum, which fails with negatives
Negatives cannot be stored in an array

questions.explanation: The window slides forward assuming that removing left elements lowers the sum. Negative numbers break that monotonicity, so those problems need prefix sums with a hash map or a deque instead.

questions.prompt: A 2-D prefix-sum (integral image) answers the sum of any axis-aligned submatrix in:
questions.explanation: Precomputing cumulative sums over the grid lets a rectangle sum be found by inclusion-exclusion of four corner values in constant time. It is widely used in image processing.

questions.prompt: The difference-array technique makes which operation O(1)?

options.text: Adding a constant to every element of a range, deferring the final values to one pass

questions.explanation: Recording +v at the start of a range and -v just past its end lets many range updates be applied in O(1) each, then a single prefix-sum pass reconstructs the array. It is the inverse of a prefix sum.

questions.prompt: In a fixed-size sliding window of width k over n elements, how many total element additions and removals occur?

options.text: O(n) — each element enters and leaves at most once

questions.explanation: As the window advances one step, exactly one element enters and one leaves, so across the whole scan there are O(n) updates. This amortised bound is what makes the technique linear.

questions.prompt: Which problem is NOT a natural fit for a simple sliding window over a contiguous range?

options.text: Smallest subarray with sum at least a target (non-negative values)
Maximum sum of any k consecutive elements
Longest substring with at most two distinct characters

questions.explanation: A subsequence need not be contiguous, so a window over a contiguous range cannot capture it — that problem needs DP or patience sorting. The others all concern contiguous subarrays or substrings.
